items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Jerry Wexler, who is a good friend of mine in Florida

ctx.x: I think it was the Drifters.

Yeah, I believe you’re right. The session included Jerry Wexler, who is a good friend of mine in Florida, he’s long retired, he points out that that session with the Drifters produced four hits. Not only “White Christmas” but “The Bells of St. Mary,” and two others which I can’t name. In those days you know, it was customary to do four numbers in a session. Now people take a month to do something and they track it and they change it and they mess around with it. Well the union contract specified four numbers in…

You had said that. “we said to each other at that time in twenty years” — this was 1955 or so — “in twenty years people will say to each other ‘listen darling, they’re playing our song.’ You know that’s exactly what happened. All that funny music that we laughed at became classic rock.”

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I played a lot of stuff for Atlantic Records — Jerry Wexler and —

ctx.x: He was for a while. And Chuck Berry and those guys.

We all — studio musicians were expected to play everything and I found that I could fit into that kind of stuff because I knew how to play boogie woogie and blues piano from my big brother’s record collection. I played a lot of stuff for Atlantic Records — Jerry Wexler and —
What kind of people did you play behind?
